sentences.text: The skull of this bird was near triangular in side view and featured a robust, toothless, and pointed beak.
Its total length was about 50 cm, with a wingspan reaching up to 70 cm.
While it possessed advanced traits like a short tail with a pygostyle and a bony sternum, it retained primitive features such as large forelimb claws and a skull with a closed eye-socket.
Several hundred complete specimens have been found, making it one of the most abundant vertebrates in the Yixian Formation.
In a specimen weighing only 0.5 kg, the primary wing feathers reached 20.7 cm in length.
It was the first early bird fossil to show preserved pheomelanosomes, though a second team failed to find these traces.
Researchers suggested that the presence of medullary bone in a specimen indicated it was a female, as this tissue serves as a calcium reservoir for egg production in modern birds.
A studied female specimen showed evidence of at least three years of growth, indicating an extended development period similar to non-avian dinosaurs.
The genus was formally described by Hou and colleagues in 1995.
The discovery began in November 1993 when paleontologists Hou Lianhai and Hu Yoaming were shown a fossil bird specimen by collector Zhang He.
The species Confuciusornis chuonzhous was named by Hou in 1997 using specimen IVPP V10919, which was originally a paratype of C. sanctus.
In 1999, researchers suggested Confuciusornis was likely herbivorous based on its upward-curving, non-raptorial beak, although no stomach contents were known at the time.
It possessed large fleshy foot pads and curved claws similar to modern tree-dwelling birds, suggesting it may have had a similar lifestyle.
The flight apparatus was more developed than that of Archaeopteryx, with some specimens showing a keel on the sternum similar to that of modern birds.
It is the oldest flying dinosaur with an almost modern flight apparatus.
In 2016, Luis Chiappe and Meng Qingjin estimated a maximum egg diameter of 23 mm based on the pelvic aperture of a large specimen.
In 2007, Gary Kaiser argued that Confuciusornis likely nested in tree crevices rather than open nests and that the small egg size suggests large clutch sizes.
Small individuals possessed long tail feathers, suggesting that sexual maturity was reached well before the animals achieved their maximum size.
Analysis of fibrous lamellae indicates that early birds possessed rapid growth phases and high metabolic rates, contrary to previous acceptance.
Paleontologist Dieter S. Peters compared Confuciusornis to the white-tailed tropicbird, noting similarities in long tails, narrow wings, and nesting habits near volcanoes.
Forty individuals were found on a 100 m² surface, suggesting entire flocks were killed by volcanic ash, heat, or gas.
Female mate choice in Confuciusornis may have been efficient if males participated in chick care, such as protecting the offspring.
The genus was established by Hou and colleagues in 1995.
Hou assigned Confuciusornis to the family Confuciusornithidae in 1995.
The recognized species include C. sanctus, C. dui, C. chuonzhous, and C. suniae, with the latter two possibly being synonyms of C. sanctus.
It lived in China between 125 and 120 million years ago during the Early Cretaceous Period.
Unlike most species found in the Yixian Formation, Confuciusornis jianchangensis was discovered in the Jiufotang Formation.
Fossils were discovered in the Yixian and Jiufotang Formations and are part of the Jehol Biota.
It is debated whether two paratype specimens belong to Confuciusornis sanctus because their bones do not overlap with the holotype.

A 2011 statistical analysis suggested that differences in C. dui might be individual variations within C. sanctus rather than distinct species, though the validity remains debated due to the potential loss of the holotype.
